slides.heading: Resistance quick hits
bullets: **Aminoglycosides**: bacterial transferases inactivate the drug (acetylation, phosphorylation, adenylation)
**Tetracyclines**: ↓ uptake or ↑ efflux via plasmid-encoded pumps
**Macrolides**: methylation of the 23S rRNA binding site

slides.heading: Classic NBME trap
slides.text: Aminoglycosides need **oxygen** to enter bacteria, so they do not work against anaerobes.
slides.detail: Cell wall inhibitors (e.g. beta-lactams) increase their entry, which is why the combination is synergistic.

slides.stem: A 68-year-old man receiving an IV antibiotic for vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium bacteremia is started on sertraline for depression. Two days later he develops agitation, hyperthermia, diaphoresis and inducible clonus. Which best describes the mechanism of his antibiotic?
options: Binds 30S subunit and causes mRNA misreading
Binds 30S subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment
Binds 50S subunit and prevents formation of the initiation complex

slides.explanation: Linezolid (used for VRE and MRSA) binds the 50S subunit and prevents formation of the initiation complex. It is also a weak **MAO inhibitor**, so adding an SSRI can trigger **serotonin syndrome**.

caption.hook: Protein synthesis inhibitors for USMLE Step 1: 30S vs 50S antibiotics in one mnemonic
body: 30S: aminoglycosides and tetracyclines. 50S: chloramphenicol, clindamycin, macrolides and linezolid.
NBME loves pairing the mechanism with the classic toxicity in one vignette, so learn them together.
Linezolid + SSRI = serotonin syndrome. Chloramphenicol = gray baby syndrome. Clindamycin = C. difficile.
